documents.title: Consensus statement on concussion in sport sixth international conference Amsterdam

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Soccer is one of the most popular sports worldwide and is a contact sport in which players are at risk of head injuries and concussions ( , ). The reported incidence of concussions is 0.27–0.41 per 1,000 athletic exposures for school-aged girls and 0.17–0.19 per 1,000 athletic exposures for school-aged boys ( , ). Head injuries can result from contact between the head and another player's head or body parts, the ground, a goal post, or head-to-ball contact ( , , ). A concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a direct blow to the head, neck, or another part of the body ( ). A concussive injury triggers a cascade of molecular alterations, including elevated neurotransmitter release, altered ion flux, hyperglycolysis, and various other metabolic shifts. These complex metabolic disturbances can result in either transient or prolonged neurological deficits. Consequently, concussions must be identified immediately to prevent subsequent injury and mitigate the risk of persistent symptoms ( ). Any athlete suspected of sustaining a concussion must be immediately (on field) evaluated using a standardized tool i.e., CFRP which includes validated modified Maddock's questions to explore orientation and memory. Furthermore, the injured player should be withdrawn from play, monitored for worsening effects, and be encouraged to rest until asymptomatic ( – ). Any athlete suspected of sustaining a concussion must undergo an immediate on-field evaluation using a standardized tool, such as the Concussion Fast Recognition Protocol (CFRP). This protocol includes validated Modified Maddocks Questions (MMQ) designed to assess orientation and memory. Furthermore, the injured player must be withdrawn from play, monitored for any worsening of symptoms, and encouraged to rest until they are completely asymptomatic ( – ). Based on the preceding data, the CFRP was utilized for the current study. However, it is important to note that the CFRP is not sport-specific and has not yet been validated in Spanish-speaking populations. While the CFRP has previously been used to identify concussions in soccer players, there are currently no data to validate its application in children ( – ). Furthermore, the Maddocks questions are primarily intended for the on-field evaluation of athletes aged 12 years and older who do not present with obvious signs of concussion ( ). The primary objective of this study is to determine the minimum age at which the Modified Maddocks Questions (MMQ) can be reliably applied to soccer players, facilitating the future validation of the Concussion Fast Recognition Protocol (CFRP) in children. We hypothesized that 1) Both comprehension and response accuracy would increase with age across the 4–8-year range. 2) Questions involving the recall of past events would yield lower accuracy compared to orientation-based questions, even among non-concussed children. 2 Methods We conducted an observational, descriptive, cross-sectional study among youth soccer players in Montevideo, Uruguay, using an adapted version of the Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT). The study took place between July and October 2024. Following authorization from the Secretaria Nacional de Deporte and approval from the respective club academies, participating teams were selected via random sampling. All participants remained anonymous throughout the process. 2.1 Participant selection and criteria Athletes were eligible if they were between the ages of 4 and 8, reflecting the early entry age for organized soccer in Uruguay ( ). Exclusion criteria consisted of: Pre-existing neurocognitive deficits. Suspected or confirmed concussion sustained during the match prior to testing. Lack of parental/guardian informed consent or player assent. 2.2 Data collection and administration The MMQT was administered orally by trained investigators during the halftime break to evaluate baseline cognitive function, attention, and comprehension in a non-injured population. To ensure objectivity, the investigators maintained no prior relationship with the participating clubs. Each assessment lasted between 1 and 3 min. If a child provided an incorrect response, the question was reformulated to further assess their capacity for comprehension vs. simple misinterpretation. Data, including gender, age, and club affiliation, were recorded in an electronic spreadsheet. Responses to each of the five MMQT questions were classified as either correct or incorrect. 2.3 Statistical analysis For data processing, participants were stratified into one-year age intervals. For each age group, we calculated the proportion of correct vs. incorrect responses and evaluated the overall comprehension levels for each of the five specific MMQT items ( ). 2.4 Ethical statement The study protocol and informed consent procedures were approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the School of Medicine at the University of the Republic, Uruguay. 2.5 Patient and public involvement Given the study design, patient and public involvement (PPI) was not required during the planning or execution phases of this research. 2.6 Statistical analysis To examine the association between age and both MMQT response accuracy (correct vs. incorrect) and question comprehension (understood vs. not understood), we employed either the Chi-square ( χ 2) test or Fisher's exact

In cases where significant associations were detected, post-hoc pairwise comparisons of proportions were performed. To account for multiple comparisons and reduce the risk of Type I errors, p -values were adjusted using the Bonferroni correction ( ). We also evaluated the association between age and the MMQT variables using logistic regression models, with age as the predictor and each question as a separate binary dependent variable. To estimate the probability of false negative or false positive outcomes based on the number of incorrect responses, we employed a binomial distribution. This calculation assumed independence between responses and utilized the mean probability of an incorrect answer across the questionnaire. The internal consistency of the MMQT was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha. In doing so, we acknowledged that the tool was originally developed as a brief clinical screening instrument rather than a unidimensional psychometric scale. Given the exploratory and descriptive nature of this study, no formal a priori sample size calculation was performed. Instead, the sample size was determined pragmatically based on participant availability and feasibility during the study period. The final cohort ( n = 88) was deemed sufficient to estimate comprehension and response accuracy with acceptable precision across the target age range. With this sample, proportions near 90% could be estimated with a margin of error of approximately ±6%–7%. Additionally, this sample size provided approximately 80% power to detect a moderate effect size (Cramer's V ≈ 0,30) in the chi-square analyses. Statistical analyses were performed using JASP (version 0.18.3). For all tests, a p -value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3 Results The study involved 88 males, aged 4 to 8 years, from six different youth soccer clubs. The distribution of children by age was as follows: 1 child aged 4, 9 children aged 5, 23 children aged 6, 33 children aged 7, and 22 children aged 8. Although all youth soccer clubs in Montevideo accept both sexes, within the age ranges chosen for the study, none of the randomly selected teams had girls on their roster. summarizes the proportion of children who correctly answered and understood each Modified Maddocks Question (MMQ) by age group. Fisher's exact test revealed no statistically significant association between age and either the accuracy of responses or comprehension of questions. Similar findings were obtained using logistic regression models with age as a predictor. However, results should be interpreted cautiously due to the small number of participants in the 4- and 5-year-old groups. When considering the total number of correct responses (range 0-5), the Spearman correlation between age and total score was 0,193 (95% CI: −0,017; 0.387), indicating no association. Conclusions cannot be generalized to 4-year-olds based on the single participant in that group. Not all participants answered every question correctly ( ); rather, question 4, showed significantly different proportion of correct responses. In contrast, comprehension rates were similar across all questions. The proportion of correct responses to question 4 was significantly lower compared to the other questions ( ). This suggests it may be more difficult or less clearly understood. Internal consistency of the five MMQT items was explored using Cronbach's alpha. The overall alpha coefficient was 0,668 (95% CI: 0.556; 0.779), indicating moderate internal consistency. When Question 4 was excluded, Cronbach's alpha decreased to 0,561, suggesting that this item did not reduce overall scale coherence. It should be noted that the MMQ is intended as a brief clinical screening tool rather than a unidimensional psychometric scale; therefore, internal consistency estimates should be interpreted cautiously. The analysis performed in for the comparison of correct responses was not carried out for language comprehension, as no association was found between the two variables ( p = 0.955, ). To evaluate the potential for diagnostic error based on the number of incorrect answers, we used the binomial distribution, if each question has the same probability of being answered incorrectly under normal (non-concussed) conditions. Based on responses to Questions 1, 2, 3, and 5, the estimated probability of an incorrect answer was 0.193. shows the probability of each of incorrect answers and its corresponding estimated diagnostic error frequency. Based on responses to Questions 1, 2, 3, and 5, the estimated probability of an incorrect answer was 0.193. shows the probability of each of incorrect answers and its corresponding estimated diagnostic error frequency. For example, if a player answers all four questions correctly, the probability of a false negative (i.e., allowing a concussed player to continue) is 42.4%. Conversely, if a child is removed from the field after just one incorrect answer, the false positive rate (i.e., removing a healthy player) is 40.6%. This rate drops significantly as the number of incorrect responses increases. This analysis excluded Question 4 due to its significantly lower correct response rate, which could reflect factors unrelated to cognitive status. Excluding question 4, If the child answered all questions correctly, the probability of continuing to play despite having sustained a concussion (false negative) is 1 in 1.7. If the child is removed from the field after one incorrect answer, the probability of error (removing the child without a concussion) is 1 in 2.5. The probability of error decreases significantly if the child provides an increasing number of incorrect answers ( ). 4 Discussion Reports of sports-related concussions, particularly in soccer, have increased in prevalence over the last decade. This trend is likely driven by enhanced diagnostic surveillance, heightened public awareness, and targeted education for parents, coaches, and athletes. Furthermore, the rising competitiveness of youth soccer has contributed to higher injury rates ( ). Among school-aged children, it is estimated that over 50% of concussions occur during recreational play ( ). In most competitive settings, certified athletic trainers serve as the primary responders for the initial assessment and management of these injuries. In recreational sports settings, however, it is essential that parents and coaches possess the necessary knowledge to recognize concussion symptoms ( ). The Concussion Fast Recognition Protocol (CFRP), implemented in 2014, was originally designed for adult athletes; consequently, there remains a lack of data regarding its utility and efficacy in pediatric populations ( ). Our findings indicate no significant association between the three primary parameters investigated: age, auditory comprehension, and the frequency of correct responses. Notably, most of the study population consisted of children aged 6, 7, and 8 years, with a smaller representation of younger participants (one 4-year-old and nine 5-year-olds). Crucially, no statistically significant differences in performance were observed among the children in the 6–8 age range. Across all age groups, participants demonstrated a high degree of language comprehension (≥96%), providing correct answers in most instances. However, Question 4 consistently yielded incorrect responses across the cohort. This finding suggests that Question 4 may be unsuitable for this specific age group; we recommend its exclusion from the protocol should further studies confirm these preliminary results. Consequently, any child failing to provide a correct response to the remaining items should be managed with a high degree of clinical suspicion and, as a precautionary measure, removed from play for formal medical assessment and rest. The Maddocks questions were originally developed for professional Australian rules football players. The initial 14-item tool assessed orientation and recent memory and was typically administered within 10 min of a suspected concussion or upon the patient regaining consciousness ( , , ). Historically, and consistent with our observations regarding Question 4, items evaluating recent memory have proven more sensitive in distinguishing between concussed and non-concussed athletes, whereas questions assessing remote events often proved challenging for all players, regardless of injury status ( , ). To the best of our knowledge, there are no published reports on the Spanish validation of the Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT) for young children, although it is a recognized instrument for differentiating between concussed and non-concussed adolescents and adults during the acute phase of injury. Since its inception in 2005, the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT) has undergone several revisions, consistently including the Maddocks questions as a core component ( ). However, research has highlighted significant performance variations linked to demographic variables, as well as cultural and linguistic differences ( , , ). While the SCAT is a standardized tool with universal applicability across disciplines including soccer, hockey, basketball, and American football, its development and validation have been most robustly established within rugby ( – ). It is therefore critical to recognize that a literal translation of the SCAT may be inadequate; cultural and linguistic adaptations are essential to ensure effective communication and prevent clinical misunderstandings ( ). The impact of language on concussion evaluation in youth athletes remains poorly understood ( ). Studies utilizing the Child

variations linked to demographic variables, as well as cultural and linguistic differences ( , , ). While the SCAT is a standardized tool with universal applicability across disciplines including soccer, hockey, basketball, and American football, its development and validation have been most robustly established within rugby ( – ). It is therefore critical to recognize that a literal translation of the SCAT may be inadequate; cultural and linguistic adaptations are essential to ensure effective communication and prevent clinical misunderstandings ( ). The impact of language on concussion evaluation in youth athletes remains poorly understood ( ). Studies utilizing the Child SCAT5 have found that Spanish-speaking children even when evaluated in English reported fewer symptoms and performed worse on specific subtests compared to their English-speaking peers. These discrepancies may be attributed to social determinants of health, such as socioeconomic status and acculturation, or inherent psychometric limitations of the tool. This underscores the need for pediatric concussion instruments to account for cultural and linguistic nuances to ensure diagnostic validity ( ). Notably, while the MMQT has been validated in Chinese, Arabic, and Italian within various SCAT versions, a Spanish pediatric validation remains a critical gap ( – ). Athletic trainers and specialized healthcare personnel are in short supply in child sports. Therefore, it is necessary to raise awareness and provide training on the use of CRT6 to all adults supervising child/adolescent sports. The CRT6 created by the Concussion in Sport Group (CISG) has been translated into several languages ( ). This study supports the utility of a Spanish-adapted MMQT for concussion screening in children aged 5–8 years. Comprehension was consistently high across age groups, although the ability to answer correctly was variable especially for questions involving recall of past events (e.g., Question 4). Previous studies on the original Maddock questions have similarly reported that items involving recall of past events are less discriminative and more variable, even among older athletes ( ). In contrast, orientation-based questions (e.g., field, half of match) rely on immediate contextual awareness and appear more robust across age groups. Given the lower performance on Question 4 despite high comprehension, its exclusion from the MMQT for this age group is recommended. While the study was limited to male athletes and had limited representation among 4- and 5-year-olds, the results are promising. Future research should expand validation to girls, younger children, and other sports. Given the limited availability of trained medical staff at youth sports events, tools like MMQT must be easily understood by non-medical adults (e.g., parents, coaches) and appropriately adapted to cultural and linguistic contexts. 4.1 Clinical implications Identifying concussions in the pediatric population remains a formidable diagnostic challenge, largely due to the communication barriers inherent to early cognitive development and a paucity of validated assessment tools. In this context, the present study offers novel and clinically significant evidence by demonstrating the feasibility of the Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT) for use among Spanish-speaking children aged 5 to 8 years. 4.2 Limitations This study is subject to several limitations. First, the sample consisted exclusively of male participants, as the randomly selected teams within the target age range lacked female players; consequently, these findings may not be generalizable to female athletes. Second, the younger cohorts were underrepresented comprising only one 4-year-old and nine 5-year-olds which limits the strength of the conclusions for these specific age groups. Third, the relatively small, convenience-based sample size may have reduced statistical power, particularly for subgroup analyses. Furthermore, the cross-sectional design and administration of the MMQT in a non-concussed setting during halftime may not fully capture the ecological validity of actual sideline conditions following a head injury. The practice of reformulating incorrect answers to assess comprehension, while helpful, may have introduced a degree of researcher subjectivity. Finally, as the MMQT has not been formally validated in Spanish-speaking pediatric populations, cultural or contextual factors may further limit its broader application. Future research incorporating larger, more diverse cohorts is warranted. 5 Conclusions Modified Maddocks Questions Tool (MMQT) is a feasible sideline concussion screening instrument for Spanish-speaking male athletes aged 5 to 8 years. However, due to its consistently lower accuracy in this demographic, we recommend that Question 4 be excluded from routine use. Clinically, any child who provides one or more incorrect responses should be immediately removed from play and referred for a comprehensive medical evaluation.

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Blood-based biomarkers such as glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) and NFL are used to detect acute neural injury after sport-related concussion, yet limited research has examined preseason baseline concentrations in contact or collision sport athletes or potential sex differences. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Female collegiate contact and collision sport athletes demonstrated higher baseline GFAP and NFL concentrations than males, whereas ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L1 and total tau did not differ by sex. Exposure-related variables, such as age of first exposure and time since most recent concussion, were not associated with biomarker levels. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY These findings identify biological sex as a source of variability in select brain-derived biomarkers and suggest that sex should be considered in future biomarker validation and longitudinal research. Introduction Repetitive head impacts (RHI) are head impacts that do not result in the clinical diagnostic criteria of concussion but may trigger complex cellular and molecular processes that evolve following the initial or repeated exposure. In recent years, there has been growing concern that exposure to RHI is detrimental to long-term neurological health and linked to functional deficits such as blood-brain barrier dysfunction, abnormal neurometabolic responses, aggregation of tau or amyloid protein, increased risk of developing chronic traumatic encephalopathy, depression and other symptoms. Unfortunately, RHI exposure is a standard component of both contact and collision sport participation, ranging from hundreds to thousands of impacts over the course of a season, depending on the position and level of play. This is especially concerning considering that fewer than 2000 RHI have been associated, in a dose-response relationship, with later-life neurological deficits. RHI and its possible link to traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (TES), the clinical disorder related to neuropathologically diagnosed chronic traumatic encephalopathy, has also received recent attention. One of the four diagnostic criteria for TES is substantial exposure to RHI’s (ie, a minimum of 5 years of organised contact/collision sport, with at least two of those years occurring at the high school level or beyond). The potential societal and economic implications of RHI are significant. Therefore, we must seek objective measures to detect early changes caused by career RHI. Previously, an earlier age of first exposure to contact/collision sports (<12 years of age) was proposed as causing later life neurodegeneration ; however, these early studies were not able to be replicated. Thus, within the current TES consensus statement, career duration is the only modifiable risk factor. Young physically active athletes may have sufficient cognitive reserves, compensatory neurocognitive capabilities or neural plasticity to adapt and overcome potential RHI-related neurotrauma. Further, the forces generated by younger athletes may not be sufficient to initiate the neurometabolic, anatomic or other injury mechanisms. Clinical measures (eg, neurocognition, balance) often fail to detect meaningful group-level differences in clinical performance or symptom presentation in collegiate contact/collision sport athletes during baseline testing. In contrast, neuroimaging studies have demonstrated RHI-related alterations in brain structure and function even in young athletes. Inflammation plays a vital role in both the repair and neurodegenerative processes following RHI; however, it can be challenging to characterise due to the invasive nature, cost and limited feasibility of direct central nervous system assessment in active athletes. Peripheral blood samples provide meaningful information about neuroinflammation in a safe, cost-effective manner. Several brain-derived biomarkers (BDM), including glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP), NFL, ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) and total tau, have successfully identified the course of neuronal, axonal and astroglial damage following concussion. RHI may worsen these processes by priming microglial cells, leading to an exaggerated inflammatory reaction on subsequent head trauma. Chronic inflammation from RHI exposure can potentially exacerbate neuronal injury, causing further degeneration and resulting in a more significant accumulation of neurofibrillar tangles and amyloid plaques, both of which may be related to neurodegenerative diseases. While amyloid and tau accumulation are established in Alzheimer’s disease, their relevance to RHI-related changes in young athletes remains unclear and speculative at this stage. In this context, baseline serum concentrations of GFAP, NFL, total tau and UCH-L1 may offer insight into individual biological sensitivity to head impact exposure, even in the absence of overt concussion symptoms. Sex differences have been documented in both concussion and neurocognitive disorders. Females who experience RHI may have poorer executive function and an elevated risk of depression compared with non-contact athletes. In later life, women are at increased risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases independent of RHI exposure, supporting underlying neurophysiological sex differences. Despite these concerning neurobehavioural and pathological findings in females, current RHI literature focuses primarily on clinical data, with later-life samples largely consisting of former male collision sport athletes. Sex differences in biomarkers may advance our understanding of injury heterogeneity and the complexity of RHI and reveal sex-dependent pathobiological processes and disease mechanisms. Many consequences of RHI remain to be elucidated,

Females who experience RHI may have poorer executive function and an elevated risk of depression compared with non-contact athletes. In later life, women are at increased risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases independent of RHI exposure, supporting underlying neurophysiological sex differences. Despite these concerning neurobehavioural and pathological findings in females, current RHI literature focuses primarily on clinical data, with later-life samples largely consisting of former male collision sport athletes. Sex differences in biomarkers may advance our understanding of injury heterogeneity and the complexity of RHI and reveal sex-dependent pathobiological processes and disease mechanisms. Many consequences of RHI remain to be elucidated, including objective measures in current athletes and stronger consideration of sex differences. Therefore, the purpose of this study is twofold: (1) to examine whether serum concentrations of four brain-derived biomarkers (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau) differ by biological sex while accounting for exposure-related variables, including age of first exposure (AFE) to contact sports and time since most recent concussion, and (2) to evaluate whether AFE and time since concussion are associated with biomarker concentrations in a subsample of collegiate football athletes. We hypothesised that serum concentrations of brain-derived biomarkers would differ by biological sex, with females exhibiting higher levels than males and that exposure-related variables, including an earlier age of first exposure and shorter time since most recent concussion, would be associated with elevated biomarker concentrations. Material and methods This cross-sectional study was a secondary analysis from the multicentre, prospective study conducted by the National Collegiate Athletic Association and the US Department of Defense Concussion Assessment, Research and Education (CARE) Consortium at the six CARE Advanced Research Core sites, including the US Military and Air Force Academies between 14 October 2014 and 30 August 2018. The Medical College of Wisconsin Institutional Review Board (IRB) and the local IRB and Human Research Protection Office at each performance site reviewed and approved all study procedures. All potential participants provided written informed consent. The inclusion criteria were incoming male and female athletes participating in contact and collision sports. Exclusion criteria included a current concussion diagnosis. A lifetime history of concussion did not exclude participants. A total of 700 college athletes (male=548/700, 78.3%) were included in the analysis ( ). Patient and public involvement Former collegiate athletes were consulted during the parent CARE Consortium study to provide input on study design and data collection logistics. Patients or members of the public were not involved in the conduct, reporting or dissemination plans specific to this secondary analysis. The detailed procedures for demographic information and blood sample acquisition have been previously described. Briefly, following participants’ consent at preseason baseline testing, non-fasting blood samples were collected by venipuncture. Using a 10 mL red top Serum Tube (Becton Dickinson, New Jersey, USA), samples were left to clot and centrifuged at 1,500 g for 15 min within 60 min of collection. Next, samples were aliquoted and stored at −80°C until shipment on dry ice to a central repository. Biomarker serum levels were quantified using the Quanterix Simoa (Lexington, Massachusetts, USA) Neuro 4-Plex B (N4PB) multiplex assay, which simultaneously measured GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau concentrations. At present, there are no established clinical thresholds or reference cut-offs for ‘elevated’ or ‘reduced’ concentrations of GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 or total tau in healthy or asymptomatic athletic populations; therefore, BDM concentrations were interpreted as relative to group differences rather than absolute clinical significance. Age of first exposure to contact or collision sports The AFE was calculated based on participants’ self-reports of when they began participating in contact or collision sports. If an athlete participated in multiple contact or collision sports concurrently, AFE was defined as the earliest age at which they began participating in any of these sports. Cumulative years of exposure were not double-counted across multiple sports. Sport was categorised based on the primary contact or collision sport in which the athlete was actively participating as a collegiate student-athlete at the time of baseline testing. Although many participants reported prior participation in multiple contact or collision sports, exposure history from earlier sport participation was captured through AFE, which reflected the earliest age at which the athlete began participating in any contact or collision sport. For example, if an athlete began playing soccer at age 6 and football at age 8, with both sports played through age 18, their AFE was recorded as six. AFE was included as a continuous variable in all general linear models. Statistical analyses Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarise participant characteristics, including biological sex, age, sport, concussion history, AFE and time since most recent concussion. To address our primary aim, a series of general linear models were conducted separately for each neuroinflammatory biomarker (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau). Each model included biological sex, sport (ie, hockey, soccer, lacrosse, rugby), AFE, time since most recent concussion

Statistical analyses Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarise participant characteristics, including biological sex, age, sport, concussion history, AFE and time since most recent concussion. To address our primary aim, a series of general linear models were conducted separately for each neuroinflammatory biomarker (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1 and total tau). Each model included biological sex, sport (ie, hockey, soccer, lacrosse, rugby), AFE, time since most recent concussion (days) and a sex-by-sport interaction term as independent variables. Effect sizes were reported using partial eta squared (η²), with benchmarks for small (0.01), medium (0.06) and large (0.14) effects. To address our second aim, separate univariate regression models were conducted within the subsample of football athletes. These models assessed whether AFE or time since their most recent concussion was associated with biomarker concentrations. Given that American football has been shown to involve particularly high cumulative exposure to repetitive head impacts relative to other contact and collision sports, and because exposure characteristics vary widely by position and individual participation patterns, we conducted a secondary subgroup analysis of football athletes to evaluate exposure-related associations within this sport specifically. This subgroup analysis complements our broader examination across all sports without implying that football is the primary focus of the study. All statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, V.29.0 (IBM, Armonk, New York, USA). Statistical significance was defined a priori at α=0.05. Adjusted R ² values were reported to reflect model fit and account for the number of predictors in each model. Biomarker distributions were visually inspected prior to analysis. Based on inspection of distributions and residual plots, biomarker concentrations were analysed on their original scale. Model assumptions of linearity, normality of residuals and homoscedasticity were evaluated and deemed acceptable for the present analyses. Formal adjustment for multiple comparisons was not applied. All analyses were specified a priori and focused on biologically distinct biomarkers that reflect different cellular and injury-related processes rather than multiple tests of a single outcome. Applying conservative corrections across these outcomes would substantially increase the risk of type II error. Accordingly, results were interpreted cautiously, with emphasis placed on effect sizes and consistency of findings across biomarkers rather than statistical significance alone. Results Aim 1: Sex and exposure-related differences in biomarkers Across the full sample of contact and collision sport athletes, sex significantly predicted GFAP and NFL concentrations. Females exhibited higher serum GFAP ( F 1,113 =15.88, p<0.001, η²=0.123) and NFL ( F 1,113 =4.92, p=0.029, η²=0.042) levels than males ( ). The overall model explained a relatively small proportion of variance in GFAP (adjusted R ²=0.069) and NFL (adjusted R ²=0.051). No significant main effects were observed for sport, AFE or time since most recent concussion for either biomarker. Interaction effects (sex×sport) were also non-significant. For UCH-L1 and total tau, sex, sport and AFE did not reach statistical significance ( and 4). The models explained minimal variance (UCH-L1: adjusted R ²=–0.023; total tau: adjusted R ²=–0.012). Aim 2: Football-Specific Exposure Associations Univariate regression models revealed no significant associations between biomarker concentrations and either AFE or time since the most recent concussion. Across all four biomarkers (GFAP, NFL, UCH-L1, total tau), model fits were poor ( R ² range=0.004–0.027), with adjusted R ² values near or below zero. Discussion The effects of RHI across a career have primarily been examined in older male former football players or healthy young collegiate athletes using clinical measures ; however, neuroimaging studies in current contact and collision sport athletes have also demonstrated RHI-related alterations in brain structure and function. Accordingly, the present study investigated objective blood-derived biomarkers in a diverse sample of active athletes without a current concussion. The primary finding of this study was that female student-athletes had significantly higher BDM serum concentrations of NFL and GFAP than their male counterparts, independent of AFE and time since the most recent concussion. Results from our study do not support a relationship between AFE and BDM serum concentration in a sample of apparently healthy young adults. Although prior studies examining career duration have reported limited associations with clinical outcomes among current athletes, the present findings extend this literature by demonstrating that sex-based differences in blood-derived biomarkers are evident even when exposure is operationalised by age at first exposure and time since the most recent concussion rather than by career duration. Although this study examined exposure-related factors, it is important to emphasise that the variables used (ie, AFE, sport category and time since most recent concussion) are indirect and relatively coarse proxies for cumulative RHI exposure. These metrics do not capture the substantial heterogeneity in head impact frequency, magnitude, position-specific exposure or duration across

reported limited associations with clinical outcomes among current athletes, the present findings extend this literature by demonstrating that sex-based differences in blood-derived biomarkers are evident even when exposure is operationalised by age at first exposure and time since the most recent concussion rather than by career duration. Although this study examined exposure-related factors, it is important to emphasise that the variables used (ie, AFE, sport category and time since most recent concussion) are indirect and relatively coarse proxies for cumulative RHI exposure. These metrics do not capture the substantial heterogeneity in head impact frequency, magnitude, position-specific exposure or duration across and within sports. As such, the absence of associations between these exposure-related variables and biomarker concentrations may not fully reflect the complex relationship between RHI exposure and biological outcomes. Despite women making up approximately 44% of all college athletes, females remain a largely understudied group in head trauma research. Our finding of significantly higher NFL and GFAP serum concentrations in female athletes suggests a potentially different underlying biological response to RHI. However, the relatively modest R 2 values (UCH-L1: adjusted R ²=–0.023; total tau: adjusted R ²=–0.012) indicate that these predictors account for only a small proportion of the variance, underscoring the need for further investigation before strong conclusions can be made. Notably, the low explained variance across models underscores that baseline biomarker concentrations are influenced by factors beyond those captured in the present analyses. GFAP is an intermediate filament protein expressed in astrocytes and serves as a marker of glial activation, particularly in response to neuroinflammatory or neurodegenerative processes. NFL, a structural component of the neuronal cytoskeleton, is released into circulation following axonal injury and is often elevated in response to trauma, vascular insult and neurodegeneration. Female sex has been associated with health disparities following a concussion, with some studies reporting females to have worse recovery outcomes, more symptoms, greater symptom severity, performed worse on neurocognitive tests, larger deficits in motor coordination, worse locomotive functioning and vestibular reflexes and took longer to recover from their concussion than males. However, it is important to note that other studies have found no significant sex differences in the clinical presentation or recovery outcome following concussion between the sexes. Sex-based differences may influence RHI-related outcomes, with potential factors including hormonal status, contraceptive use, menstrual cycle phase and lower cervical muscle strength in females. Detecting sex-specific long-term changes in BDM serum concentrations could provide researchers and clinicians with early insight into the identification of neurodegenerative diseases, further highlighting the need to investigate sex as a biological variable in long-term health outcomes from RHI. We found serum GFAP and NFL concentrations to be significantly elevated in female athletes compared with males, independent of sport, AFE and time since the most recent concussion. These findings highlight the need for future work to determine whether sex-specific reference ranges or thresholds are appropriate, particularly in longitudinal or outcome-linked studies. Interestingly, while some studies in older adults have reported higher NFL concentrations in males, our data from young, currently active athletes demonstrate the opposite pattern. This discrepancy may reflect age-related, hormonal or exposure-based differences in biomarker expression, further emphasising the importance of considering sex and chronological age when evaluating blood-based indicators of neurotrauma. Although females exhibited higher baseline GFAP and NFL concentrations, these findings may not fully reflect the complex relationship between RHI and neurobiological outcomes. Elevated baseline biomarker levels may reflect sex differences in normative biomarker physiology, including differences in body composition, blood volume, hormonal status, clearance kinetics or assay behaviour, rather than injury-related processes. Additionally, the absence of a non-contact female comparison group limits our ability to determine whether observed differences are sport-related or reflect broader sex-based physiological differences. Accordingly, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive and hypothesis-generating, warranting further investigation using appropriate control groups and longitudinal designs. Female athletes in our cohort reported an AFE almost 2 years earlier than their male counterparts, which may reflect a longer duration of exposure to contact and collision sport participation; however, patterns of head impact exposure and concussion risk differ by sport. Although extended exposure could theoretically increase vulnerability to neurodegenerative diseases, women typically do not participate in football, which accounts for the majority of head impacts, sport-related concussion (SRC) and an overwhelming percentage of the documented cases of neurodegenerative diseases. In our analysis, AFE, UCH-L1 and total tau were not significantly influenced by any of the predictors examined. Notably, the very low adjusted R ² values observed in the football subgroup analyses indicate limited explained variance, and these football-specific models should therefore be interpreted with caution and viewed as exploratory rather than definitive evidence of exposure–biomarker relationships. The absence of effects for UCH-L1 and total tau may reflect their shorter post-injury temporal windows, reduced sensitivity to cumulative subconcussive exposure or greater variability in expression across individuals. Sports-related concussion is associated with elevated BDM markers in the acute post-injury phase ; however, how these markers change over the course of a lifetime with RHI exposure remains unclear. Moreover, the combined effect of concussion history and cumulative RHI on BDM, rather than each factor alone, is still unknown. Based on the promising evidence that BDM may support the early detection, prognosis and monitoring of neurodegeneration in later life, future research should investigate how serum concentrations change with ageing and how they correlate with clinical diagnoses of neurodegenerative diseases. Consistent with our findings, prior studies have not observed significant associations between AFE and clinical outcomes. These AFE studies, based on four independent cohorts with nearly 10 000 young adult athletes across 20 outcome measures, found no meaningful relationships in clinical outcomes. To the best of our knowledge, no published studies of current athletes show a statistically significant association between AFE and worse functional or clinical outcomes following concussion. The current study yielded similar findings, in which we derived AFE from the total number of athletic seasons self-reported by athletes. Overall, we did not observe a significant relationship between AFE and BDM in current college athletes. However, the extent to which RHI, biomarkers and biological sex are related throughout the lifespan remains to be elucidated. Limitations The participants in this study were part of the Advanced Research Core of the CARE Consortium, which resulted in an unequal representation of sexes and sports. Indeed, nearly 50% of our sample consisted of football players, and there was no equivalent female collision sport comparison. However, an important strength of this study is the inclusion of male and female rugby athletes, one of the few contact sports in which the rules and contact demands are similar across sexes, allowing for more comparable examination of repetitive head impact exposure between males and females. The absence of a non-contact female control group limits direct comparisons and reduces our ability to distinguish collision-related effects from baseline sex differences. Additionally, the use of proxy measures for exposure introduces the potential for exposure misclassification, and residual confounding from unmeasured factors may have influenced observed associations. We only measured BDM serum concentrations at a single preseason time point; subsequent assessments at various time points and additional biomarkers should be considered, particularly across the lifespan and account for menstrual cycle fluctuations in premenopausal women. Future research is needed, using different populations and methodologies to better understand whether RHI is associated with differences in brain physiology or functioning, along with compensatory strategies, in the years to decades following contact and collision sports careers. Specifically, research is needed to examine the association between RHI and both clinical (eg, neurocognitive function, balance, symptom severity) and objective (eg, BDM, neuroimaging) measures across the lifespan in both men and women. Blood samples were taken from a convenience sample, and participants were not enrolled with the purpose of equal representation across all sports. Conclusion Females currently participating in contact and collision sports have significantly higher GFAP and NFL serum concentrations independent of sport, AFE and time since most recent concussion. These results underscore sex-based differences in biological sensitivity to head impact exposure and may inform future biomarker surveillance frameworks, particularly in populations with elevated RHI exposure. If biomarkers are higher in current female athletes than in males at baseline, this could play a crucial role in later-life neurological health.
